Ed. 2025, 64, e202519315 doi.org/10.1002/anie.202519315 Batteries Advanced Self-Phase-Separating Electrolytes for High-Performance Lithium-Sulfur Batteries Xu Yao+, Zhicheng Wang+,* Suwan Lu+, Haifeng Tu, Jingjing Xu, Xingdong Ma, Kun Liang, Yongbin Lin, Anqi Chen, Sicheng Xu, Ju Ren, Ke Wang, Fengrui Zhang, Jieyun Zheng, Xiaodong Wu,* and Hong Li* Abstract: Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries face a critical challenge in synergistically optimizing high-sulfur-loading redox kinetics and suppressing soluble lithium polysulfide (LiPSs) shuttle effects.

Herein, we propose a self-phaseseparating electrolyte design strategy based on heterogeneous LiPSs dissolution characteristics, using co-solvents of 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) and cyclopentyl methyl ether (CPME) to induce spontaneous phase separation during LiPSs dissolution through solvation disparity.

The constructed electrolyte system facilitates formation of a strong-solvation region at the cathode to maintain rapid sulfur redox kinetics while establishing a weak-solvation region at the anode to form a stable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), thereby achieving dual objectives of “kinetics promotion and shuttle suppression” via a spatially partitioned dual-zone synergistic mechanism.
This strategy enables steady cycling above 170 cycles of singlelayer Li-S pouch cells with ultra-thin Li anodes (50 μm) and high-sulfur-loading cathodes (4.3 mgs cm−2).

Moreover, under practical lean-electrolyte conditions (6.2 mgs cm−2 sulfur loading, 50 μm Li, 3 μL mgs−1 electrolyte), a 1.8 Ah multilayer pouch cell delivers 323 Wh kg−1 energy density with stable cycling above 50 cycles.
This work provides an effective solution for resolving the critical trade-off between rapid sulfur conversion kinetics and stable anode interfacial behavior in metal-sulfur batteries.

Introduction Amidst the urgent global demand for energy transition and carbon neutrality, developing novel energy storage technologies with ultrahigh energy density has emerged as a frontier challenge in energy science.[1,2] The lithiumsulfur (Li-S) battery system, leveraging its unique dual-highcapacity electrode characteristics of sulfur cathode (1675 mAh g−1) and Li anode (3860 mAh g−1), demonstrates a superior theoretical gravimetric energy density of 2,600 Wh kg−1, positioning it as a transformative system to surpass current energy storage limits.[3,4] The competitiveness of Li-S batteries stems from resource substitution of critical metals, compared to layered oxide cathodes reliant on lowabundance cobalt/nickel, sulfur offers a disruptive advantage through its high natural abundance and low cost.[5,6] However, the polysulfide (LiPSs) shuttle effect creates orders-ofmagnitude gaps between theoretical and practical cycling stability/discharge capacity, constituting the primary technical barrier to industrialization.[7,8] Distinct from the intercalation mechanism in conventional lithium-ion batteries, the unique solid (S8)-liquid (LiPSs)- solid (Li2S2/Li2S) multiphase reaction pathway of Li-S batteries dictates dual regulation characteristics of redox kinetics.[9,10] In the electrolyte with high LiPSs solubility, while rapid liquid-phase polysulfide conversion enhances sulfur cathode kinetics, it inevitably intensifies LiPSs diffusion toward the Li anode, triggering dual detrimental consequences.

Emerging phase-separation electrolyte strategies overcome conventional design constraints by creating nonequilibrium microenvironments.

Ren et al. proposed a biphasic system exploiting polarity differences to induce solvent stratification, high-polarity tetramethylene sulfone (TMS)- based electrolyte formed a Li+-enriched layer at the anode for optimized deposition kinetics, while low-polarity dibutyl ether (DBE) with polymeric ion conductors constructed polysulfide-blocking barriers at the cathode.[23] Despite synergistic interfacial stabilization, complex gradient fabrication (requiring preformed gel layers and precise phase-interface control) increased manufacturing costs.

Recently, Kang et al.’s self-phase-separating electrolyte (SPSE) in aqueous zinc batteries offers a new paradigm, water/non-aqueous spontaneous separation via solvent polarity regulation enables hydrophilic phases ensuring fast cathode kinetics and hydrophobic phases forming fluorinated interphases suppressing hydrogen evolution/dendrites.[24] This thermodynamics-driven selforganization simplifies preparation while achieving adaptive electrode-kinetics matching via phase-boundary modulation, providing valuable insights for Li-S systems.
However, there are few reports on the application of SPSE in Li-S batteries.

It is of great significance to conduct an in-depth analysis of its phase separation behavior and mechanism in real-time battery operation, and to promote its application in practical Li-S pouch batteries under harsh conditions.

Herein, we propose a dynamic self-phase-separating electrolyte, with 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) and cyclopentyl methyl ether (CPME) co-solvents, exploiting solvation disparity to counter LiPSs shuttle effects in conventional ether electrolytes.

Unlike homogeneous dissolution and shuttling of LiPSs in conventional ether-based electrolyte (Figure 1a), the CPME/DME system utilizes sterically hindered weakly solvating CPME and strongly solvating DME to induce spontaneous phase separation via differential LiPSs solubility (Figure 1b).

During discharging process, DME preferentially coordinates LiPSs forming cathode-localized redox-active zones ensuring efficient sulfur conversion, while CPME migrates to the Li anode interface forming in situ protective layers with dual physical-blocking and interfacial-stabilization functions.
Li-S batteries with CPME/DME electrolyte exhibit exceptional performance, single-layer pouch cells (S loading = 4.3 mgs cm−2, 50 μm Li, E/S = 6 μL mgs−1) deliver 851.7 mA h g−1 after 170 cycles.
Even under harsh conditions (S loading = 6.2 mgs cm−2, 50 μm Li, E/S = 3 μL mgs−1), 1.8 Ah multi-layer pouch cells achieve 323 Wh kg−1 initial energy density and steady cycling above 50 cycles.

Results and Discussion In conventional 1,3-dioxolane (DOL)/DME (1:1, v/v) solvents, the system maintains a single liquid phase before and after saturated Li2S8 dissolution (Figure 1c,d), indicating homogeneous LiPSs solvation characteristics.

In contrast, within the CPME/DME (1:1, v/v) solvents, steric hindrance from cyclopentyl groups substantially weakens the oxygen coordination capability of CPME molecules, reducing overall solvation power.[25] Notably, although CPME introduction was expected to decrease polysulfide solubility, experimental observations reveal no significant solubility reduction post Li2S8 dissolution.

Instead, spontaneous liquid-liquid phase separation occurs, forming a transparent light-red up phase and brick-red down phase (Figure 1e,f), with identical phenomena observed for Li2S6 and Li2S4 dissolution (Figure S1).
In order to figure out the reasons for the aforementioned phenomenon, dissolution characteristics of Li2S8 in DME, DOL, CPME, and their mixtures were systematically evaluated (Figure 1g).

The solubility of S was detected by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES), demonstrating that DME exhibits highest sulfur solubility (7.88 mol L−1), followed by the down phase of CPME/DME (3.42 mol L−1), DOL/DME (2.17 mol L−1), DOL (0.51 mol L−1), while the up phase of CPME/DME (0.26 mol L−1) and pure CPME (0.16 mol L−1) show significantly lower solubility.

Concurrently, the densities of solutions with saturated Li2S8 rank as DOL (1.21 g cm−3) > DOL/DME (1.20 g cm−3) > DME (1.15 g cm−3), with down phase (1.09 g cm−3) and up phase (0.89 g cm−3) of CPME/DME approaching pure DME (1.15 g cm−3) and pure CPME (0.88 g cm−3), respectively.
Cross-comparison confirms the sulfur content (3.42 mol L−1) and density (1.09 g cm−3) of down phase of CPME/DME align with pure DME, while these Angew.

This solubility gradient, engineered through differential LiPSs solvation capabilities, establishes the thermodynamic foundation for spatial polysulfide confinement.

Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) calculations comparing solvent-Li2S8 binding energies (Figure 2a) reveal the strongest interaction for Li2S8- DME (−439.7 kJ mol−1), followed by Li2S8-DOL (−347.1 kJ mol−1), with weakest binding for Li2S8-CPME (−271.2 kJ mol−1), confirming solvent solvation capability order: DME > DOL > CPME.
Radial distribution function (RDF) analysis from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations (Figure 2b–e) elucidates LiPSs solvation features in different mixed solvents.
In DOL/DME system (Figure 2b,d), both DOL and DME show RDF peaks at ∼1.8 Å around Li2S8 with overlapping distributions, confirming co-participation in the primary solvation shell of LiPSs.

In CPME/DME system (Figure 2c,e), DME coordinates within Li2S8’s first solvation shell (peak ∼1.8 Å) enabling effective dissolution/conversion, while the RDF curve of CPME appears beyond 4.5 Å with substantially reduced intensity.
This spatially segregated coordination indicates steric hindrance prevents CPME from competing with DME for primary coordination sites, ultimately expelling it to outer solvation regions.
Above results provide direct molecular-level evidence of heterogeneous dissolution of LiPSs in CPME/DME system.
In order to validate above results, 17O nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) chemical shift (δ) evolution upon LiPSs addition was monitored.

Larger δ changes toward higher fields indicate stronger ion-dipole interactions and nuclear shielding.[26] As shown in Figure 2f, adding Li2S8 to DOL/DME shifts DME’s 17O δ from −24.28 to −24.52 ppm (δ = 0.24 ppm), and the 17O δ of DOL shifts from 35.19 to 35.12 ppm (δ = 0.07 ppm).
In CPME/DME (Figure 2g), DME’s δ shifts from −24.00 to −24.31 ppm (δ = 0.31 ppm), while the 17O δ of CPME remains unchanged at 2.14 ppm, confirming negligible participation in LiPSs solvation.
The δ shift magnitude order (CPME < DOL < DME) reflects ion-dipole interaction strength hierarchy.

CPME’s presence forces DME to enhance ion-dipole interactions to maintain Li2S8 dissolution, which is evidenced by DME’s pronounced 17O δ shift, consistent with selective solvation and heterogeneous dissolution mechanisms.
As established in Figure 1f, CPME/DME system exhibits distinct phase separation after saturated Li2S8 dissolution.
We therefore employed 7Li NMR to monitor chemical shifts of Li2S8 in separated phases, revealing δ of 3.20 ppm in the up phase versus 1.87 ppm in the down phase (Figure 2h).

This differential shielding arises from distinct solvation environments, CPME-dominated up phase (weak solvation) versus DME-rich down phase (strong solvation), where reduced δ confirms stronger solvation Angew.

Combined with MD-derived solvation shell distributions, this corroborates selective LiPSs partitioning in CPME/DME, where CPME’s weak solvation drives preferential LiPSs enrichment in the DME phase, thereby inducing phase separation.

In order to balance the physicochemical properties (ionic conductivity, density and Li salt solubility) and the SEI filmforming performance of electrolyte, an optimized salt concentration of 0.4 M lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulphonyl) imide (LiTFSI) and 0.4 M lithium nitrate (LiNO3) was selected based on Suo’s test results.[27] Systematic adjustment of the CPME/DME volume ratio at this salt concentration revealed that electrolytes turned cloudy due to salt supersaturation when CPME content exceeded 50 vol% (Fig.
S2), indicating that an increase in the content of weakly solvating CPME solvent will reduce the dissociation ability of the electrolyte towards the salt.
Consequently, the CPME content was restricted to below 50 vol% to maintain homogeneous solution characteristics.

Within the optimized range (CPME ≤40 vol%), the electrolytes exhibit suitable physicochemical properties with viscosities remain 0.99∼1.10 mPa s and ionic conductivities reach 2.89∼5.50 mS cm−1 (Figure S3), the decrease in ionic conductivity with the increase of the CPME content also proves the weak solvation effect of CPME.
To investigate the effect of CPME content on the electrolyte solvation structure, Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy was performed (Figure S4).

Compared to pure DME-based electrolyte, after adding 40 vol% CPME, the characteristic peak of TFSI−blue-shifts from 746.4 to 748.3 cm−1 (ν = +1.9 cm−1), and the NO3−peak shifts from 1056.9 to 1058.9 cm−1 (ν = +2.0 cm−1).
This synchronous blue-shift indicates enhanced coordination between Li+ and TFSI−/NO3−, significantly increasing the proportion Angew.

Research Article of aggregate species (AGGs) and contact ion pairs (CIPs) in the electrolyte.[28] This anion-dominated solvation structure characteristic is attributable to intensified coordination competition between Li+ and anions due to CPME’s weak solvation capability.
Raman spectroscopy further elucidated CPME’s modulation mechanism on electrolyte solvation structure.

In the Raman spectra (Figure S5), the main vibration peak of TFSI−shifts from 739.3 cm−1 in pure DME-based electrolyte to 741.2 cm−1 in CPME/DME (4:6, v/v) system (ν = +1.9 cm−1), indicating enhanced coordination between Li+ and TFSI−upon CPME introduction, consistent with FTIR conclusions.

Meanwhile, the C–O stretching vibration peak of free DME appears at 850.5 cm−1, while it blueshifts to 871.9 cm−1 ascribed to Li+-coordinated DME.[14] The intensity ratio between these peaks increased monotonically with CPME content, confirming a significant reduction in free DME proportion.
This occurs because CPME’s low coordination capability forces Li+ to preferentially bind with DME molecules, decreasing free DME quantity as DME volume fraction decreases.
Notably, CPME’s characteristic Raman peak at 895 cm−1 shows no obvious shift in different electrolytes, directly verifying its weak coordination interaction with Li+.
To further investigate optimal formulations for CPME/DME electrolytes, their electrochemical performance was tested in Li-S coin cells assembled with S/C cathodes and Li metal anodes.
Electrochemical tests showed that the cycling stability and capacity retention of Li-S batteries improve monotonically with increasing CPME proportion (Figure S6).

Therefore, the electrolyte with CPME/DME = 4:6 (v/v) was ultimately selected as the optimal ratio, balancing solvation capability (DME-dominated) and interfacial stability (CPME-regulated), providing a preferred electrolyte system for subsequent battery performance evaluation.
Concurrently, comparative evaluation was conducted between the optimized CPME/DME electrolyte and conventional ether electrolyte (1 M LiTFSI in DOL/DME = 1:1 with 2% LiNO3) in Li-S batteries.

The CPME/DME electrolyte demonstrates superior rate capability in Li-S batteries compared to DOL/DME electrolyte (Figures 3a and S7), delivering discharge capacities of 1141.66, 901.93, 829.13, 791.46, 767.06, and 750.13 mA h g−1 at 0.1C, 0.2C, 0.4C, 0.6C, 0.8C, and 1C, respectively.
Upon returning to 0.1C, capacity also can recover to 918.82 mA h g−1.
Cycling stability tests (Figures 3b and S8) revealed that the CPME/DME system achieves 86.9% capacity retention after 200 cycles at 0.2C with 99.9% Coulombic efficiency.
In contrast, conventional DOL/DME system shows only 66.8% retention and 98.1% Coulombic efficiency under identical conditions.

Initial discharge curves post-activation (Figure S9) show that despite similar capacity utilization at the first plateau, rapid polarization at the second discharge plateau in DOL/DME system results in significantly lower capacity than CPME/DME system.

This may be attributed to Li2S nucleation kinetics, quantified by the potential gap between nucleation onset and discharge plateau.[29] This gap measured 32.8 mV in DOL/DME system versus only 16.6 mV in CPME/DME system, demonstrating that the dynamic phase-separation structure effectively enhances polysulfide conversion kinetics.
This optimization originates from regulation of LiPSs redox pathways by the cathode-side DME-enriched phase, promoting rapid Li2S nucleation deposition.

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) before and after cycling (Figure 3c) also confirmed that the CPME/DME system exhibits lower total impedance, correlating with its formation of more uniform and conductive SEI layer, along with low viscosity and high ionic conductivity after LiPSs dissolution (Figure S10).
At a high charge/discharge rate of 0.5C, Li-S coin cells with CPME/DME electrolyte still demonstrate excellent cycling stability (Figure 3d), achieving 76.7% capacity retention after 400 cycles.

Under harsh conditions in Li-S coin cells (50 μm ultrathin Li anode, 7 μL mgs−1 lean electrolyte, 4.3 mgs cm−2 high-loading sulfur cathode), the CPME/DME electrolyte still exhibits superior electrochemical performance (Figure 3e and Figure S11), delivering a high discharge capacity of 1152.4 mA h g−1 during initial 0.05C activation.
After three activation cycles, at 0.1C cycling rate, discharge capacity reaches 848.6 mA h g−1, maintaining 832.0 mA h g−1 after 100 cycles (98.0% retention).

With conventional DOL/DME electrolyte, initial discharge capacity at 0.1C was only 799.9 mA h g−1, decreasing to 532.7 mA h g−1 after 100 cycles (66.6% retention), significantly lower than CPME/DME system.

Charge/discharge curves at the 1st and 100th cycles (Figure 3f) indicate that the DOL/DME system exhibits rapidly increasing polarization in discharge profiles, signifying the consumption of active substances and the deterioration of the electrode interphase.

In contrast, Li-S batteries with CPME/DME electrolyte demonstrate slower polarization growth rate, suggesting reduced parasitic reactions.[30] In CPME/DME system, comparative cycling performance and charge-discharge curves further reveal slightly increased polarization, reduced Coulombic efficiency and capacity under high sulfur loading (4.1 mg cm−2 versus 1.1 mg cm−2) and thin Li (50 μm versus 400 μm) after equivalent cycling (Figure S12), indicating the feasibility of this electrolyte in practical Li-S batteries under harsh conditions.
To clarify the suppression of parasitic reactions between LiPSs and Li anodes by CPME/DME electrolyte, shuttle currents were first measured in Li-S batteries.
To amplify the shuttle effect, constant potentials were applied to cells with LiNO3-free electrolytes[31] (Figure S13).
It is found that the DOL/DME system exhibits a pronounced shuttle current peak at 2.4 V (versus Li+/Li) (0.26 mA cm−2), indicating LiPSs reduction at the anode.
In contrast, CPME/DME system maintains peak current densities below 0.05 mA cm−2 throughout the potential window, significantly lower than that of DOL/DME system.
This confirms that the CPME phase effectively blocks LiPSs diffusion to the anode via physical barrier effects, substantially weakening parasitic reaction kinetics.
Interfacial morphology characterization of cycled Li anodes (50 cycles) reveals parasitic reaction differences between electrolytes (Figure 4a).

Optical images show the CPME/DME electrolyte forms a dense, uniform SEI layer on Li metal surface without structural defects, whereas DOL/DME electrolyte exhibits extensive SEI cracking and delamination, exposing underlying pulverized Li metal.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) shows consistent results, Li deposits maintain homogeneous compact structures in CPME/DME electrolyte, while DOL/DME electrolyte displays numerous cracks and localized dendrite growth.

This morphological contrast directly verifies that CPME addition effectively inhibits chemical corrosion of SEI by polysulfides, thereby promoting uniform Li deposition and enhancing interfacial stability.
Li metal reversibility was further evaluated in asymmetric Li||Cu cells at a current density of 0.5 mA cm−2 and an areal capacity of 1.0 mA h cm−2 (Figure S14).
Compared to only 40 stable cycles in conventional DOL/DME electrolyte, CPME/DME enables steady cycling over 100 cycles, demonstrating high Li stripping/plating reversibility.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) depth profiling of cycled Li metal anode (50 cycles) elucidates electrolytedependent SEI chemistry (Figure 4c–f).
In CPME/DME system, surface sulfur content (0.18%) is significantly lower than that in DOL/DME system (0.30%).
With increasing sputtering depth (60 and 120 s), sulfur levels remain low in CPME/DME system (0.33%, 0.19%), reduced by 54% and 62% compared to that in DOL/DME system (0.72%, 0.50%) (Figure 4c).
Sulfur speciation analysis indicates trace SO32−/SO42−at the SEI surface formed in CPME/DME, but only Li2S2/Li2S reduction products are detected after 120 s sputtering depth (Figure 4d).
Conversely, DOL/DME system exhibits higher contents of Li2S2/Li2S products and retains significant SO32−signals even after 120 s etching (Figure 4e,f).

This compositional difference confirms that the CPME phase suppresses LiPSs migration to the anode and subsequent decomposition via physical blocking, constructing a sulfurlean, highly stable SEI structure.[32] Time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS) depth profiling further validates SEI compositional differences (Figure 4g,h).

Concurrently, intensified F−fragment signals in CPME/DME indicate anion (TFSI−)-dominated solvation promotes inorganic-rich SEI formation.[33] This anion-derived interphase exhibits high ionic conductivity and mechanical stability, synergistically suppressing dendrite growth and polysulfide parasitic reactions.

Comparative C2HO−fragment distribution analysis reveals high organic content in DOL/DME derived SEI originates from continuous reductive decomposition of solvents, accelerating irreversible electrolyte consumption.
In contrast, CPME/DME system suppresses solvent decomposition pathways, tailoring SEI composition toward inorganic salt-dominated stable structures.
Critically, the F 1 s and O 1 s XPS spectra (Figure S15 and S16) provide independent cross-validation of these conclusions, reinforcing the TOF-SIMS-derived mechanistic insights.

These results demonstrate that the introduction of CPME significantly reduces side-reaction activity at the electrolyte-Li metal interface by reconstructing solvation microenvironments, providing critical guarantees for longterm cycling stability in Li-S batteries.
Cyclic voltammetry (CV) further verifies electrochemical reduction behavior differences among solvents (Figure S17).
Within identical potential windows, DME exhibits the highest reduction current density (4.4 μA cm−2), followed by DOL (2.2 μA cm−2), while CPME shows a tenfold lower reduction current Angew.

Notably, no distinct reduction peaks are detected for CPME throughout the scan range, confirming exceptional anti-reductive decomposition capability.[21] The phase separation behavior and mechanism of the electrolyte in the Li-S battery in real time were observed by in situ Li-S visible cell and in situ Raman spectroscopy.
First, in situ Li-S visible cells demonstrated the existence of the phase separation phenomenon and its inhibitory effect on the shuttle effect of LiPSs as well as the corrosion of the Li anode.

The initial discharge curve of Li-S cell with CPME/DME electrolyte was shown in Figure 5a, four typical time points were selected to observe the phase separation behavior of the electrolyte under different LiPSs conditions.
As shown in Figure 5b, in the presence of long-chain LiPSs, the color of the electrolyte in S/C cathode side turns yellow due to the dissolution of LiPSs (stage A).
The phase separation leads to a distinct distribution of LiPSs.
Specifically, a dark brown phase rich in LiPSs has accumulated near the S/C cathode side, while on the Li anode side, a light yellow phase with less LiPSs has formed (stage B).

As the subsequent discharge progresses, the phase separation phenomenon of the electrolyte weakens, and the colour also becomes lighter as the long-chain LiPSs transform into solid-state shortchain LiPSs (stages C and D).
In contrast, the Li-S cell using DOL/DME electrolyte maintained a uniform colour throughout the discharge process and no phase separation was observed (Figure 5c).

Meanwhile, on the Li metal anode side, due to the presence of phase separation behavior in the CPME/DME electrolyte, less change in colour was observed compared to the DOL/DME electrolyte, which proved the inhibition of LiPSs shuttle.

By comparing the state of the Li metal electrode after discharge, it was found that the Li metal in the DOL/DME electrolyte turned significantly black, while in the CPME/DME electrolyte, the Li metal still maintained its metallic luster.
This further proves the beneficial effect of the CPME/DME electrolyte in inhibiting the corrosion of the Li metal electrode.

However, due to the relatively large E/S ratio and the considerable distance between the positive and negative electrodes in the aforementioned H-type battery, the phase separation behavior of the electrolyte may be subject to certain disturbances.
Therefore, further application of in situ Raman spectroscopy can provide a more accurate analysis of the microscopic structural changes of the electrolyte caused by phase separation.
As shown in Figure 5d, in situ Raman spectra of the CPME/DME electrolyte near the S/C cathode side were collected at various discharge states.

During the initial stage of battery discharge, the characteristic peaks of CPME solvent near the S/C cathode gradually disappeared, while the typical Raman peaks of DME coordinated with LiPSs strengthened.[14] This indicates that DME aggregated near the cathode while CPME was repelled, suggesting the occurrence of electrolyte phase separation induced by the generation of long-chain soluble LiPSs.
As the battery continues to discharge, the soluble long-chain LiPSs gradually deposited into short-chain LIPSs.
The Raman signal of the coordinated DME on the cathode side weakens, while the Raman signal of CPME reappears and gradually strengthens.
This indicates that during the depth discharge, the decrease in soluble LiPSs concentration allows the electrolyte to restore its initial homogeneous state.

Furthermore, the characteristic Raman peaks of TFSI−also demonstrated the dynamic process of electrolyte phase separation.[34] The weak solvation effect of CPME in the homogeneous phase facilitated the coordination between TFSI−and Li+.
After phase separation occurred, the reduction of CPME promoted the coordination between DME and Li+, thereby releasing more free TFSI−.

Therefore, in our opinion, the reasons for the formation of the separated phases in this work mainly stem from the difference in solubility of LiPSs in the two different solvents, which leads to differences in polarity and density of the mixed system, and subsequently results in the phase separation phenomenon.
Furthermore, additional thermodynamic driving forces, such as electric fields and chemical potential gradients, collectively contribute to the observed phase separation process.
Practicality of CPME/DME electrolyte was further evaluated under harsher conditions in Li-S pouch cells.

In singlelayer Li-S pouch cells with ultrathin Li anodes (50 μm), lean electrolyte (6 μL mgs−1), and high-loading sulfur cathodes (4.3 mgs cm−2) (Figure 6a), CPME/DME system delivered 1111.2 mA h g−1 initial discharge capacity at 0.03C activation, then the pouch cell was cycled at 0.05C.

In this condition, the first-cycle capacity of pouch cell with CPME/DME electrolyte reached 808.4 mA h g−1, maintaining 851.7 mA h g−1 after 170 cycles, with Coulombic efficiency >98% after 100 cycles and excellent reproducibility (Figure S18).

In contrast, the pouch cell with DOL/DME electrolyte sustained <100 stable cycles, exhibiting rapid capacity decay beyond 100 cycles (365.7 mA h g−1 at 118th cycle) and Coulombic efficiency dropping below 90%.

Additionally, a 1.8 Ah Li-S pouch cell was assembled with CPME/DME electrolyte under harsh conditions (S loading of each side is 6.2 mgs cm−2, match with 50 μm Li, E/S = 3 μL mgs−1) (Figure 6c,d), it achieved 323 Wh kg−1 initial energy density (based on the overall weight of the pouch cell) at 0.03C and retained above 200 Wh kg−1 after 50 cycles at 0.05C.
In contrast, the pouch cell with DOL/DME electrolyte sustained only 6 cycles before severe overcharging at 7th cycle (Figure S19).

Notably, although the Li-S pouch cell with DOL/DME showed an initial capacity similar to that of the CPME/DME system, the CPME/DME system attained superior energy density due to its lower electrolyte density (1.00 versus 1.26 g mL−1, 20% reduction).

Compared to other strategies, CPME/DME demonstrates significant potential for practical Li-S pouch cells, establishing a new electrolyte design paradigm that resolves the fundamental conflict between sulfur kinetics enhancement and anode protection in conventional electrolyte systems.
The cycling performance of Li-S coin cells and pouch cells obtained in this work was compared with recently reported literature (Tables S1 and S2).

It is found that the coin cell obtained in this work exhibits a high capacity release and exceptional capacity retention, the pouch cell obtained in this work exhibits a moderately high energy density and superior cycling lifespan.
Further optimization of sulfur cathodes combined with self-phase-separating electrolytes is projected to substantially enhance energy density and rate capability in subsequent developments.

Conclusion This study addresses the intrinsic conflict between sulfur cathode kinetics and LiPSs shuttling in Li-S batteries by innovatively proposing a dynamic phase-separation electrolyte system regulated by solvation disparity.
Constructing a binary solvent of CPME and DME leverages heterogeneous LiPSs dissolution to achieve spatial decoupling of cathode/anode interfacial microenvironments.
At the sulfur cathode, the strongly solvating DME-enriched phase maintains efficient sulfur redox kinetics.

At the Li metal anode, the weakly solvating CPME phase suppresses LiPSs diffusion via physical blocking while inducing inorganic-rich SEI formation, significantly enhancing Li deposition uniformity and interfacial stability.
Therefore, the Li-S batteries with CPME/DME electrolyte demonstrate exceptional performance even under practical conditions.
Single-layer Li-S pouch cells (50 μm Li, 4.3 mgs cm−2 high S loading, 6 μL mgs−1 lean electrolyte) show stable cycling performance over 170 cycles.
Multi-layer 1.8 Ah Li-S pouch cells (50 μm Li, 6.2 mgs cm−2 high S loading, 3 μL mgs−1 lean electrolyte) achieve 323 Wh kg−1 initial gravimetric energy density and sustain 50 stable cycles.
By spatially reconstructing solvation microenvironments, this work overcomes the mutual exclusion of sulfur kinetics and Li Angew.

Cyclopentyl Methyl Ether (CPME, 98%, Energy Chemical), 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME, battery grade, LionGo New Energy), 1,3-dixolane (DOL, battery grade, LionGo New Energy), lithium bis-(trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI, analytically pure, LionGo New Energy), and LiNO3 (99.99% metals basis, Aladdin) were used as received without further purification.
Preparation of electrolytes and electrodes The conventional DOL/DME electrolyte was prepared with 1.0 M LiTFSI and 2.0 wt.% LiNO3 dissolved in DOL/DME (1:1, by vol.).
CPME/DME electrolyte was composed of 0.4 M LiTFSI and 0.4 M LiNO3 dissolved in CPME/DME (4:6, by vol.).
Both electrolytes were prepared in an argon-filled glove box.

Sulfur/carbon nanotube (S/CNT) composites were prepared by infiltrating sublimed sulfur (battery-grade, Aladdin) into CNTs (battery-grade, Shandong Dazhan Nano Materials Co.) via a melt-diffusion method.
CNTs and pristine sulfur were ball-milled at a 1:4 mass ratio for 4 h.
The mixture was then transferred to a sealed vessel and heated at 155 °C for 10 h.
After cooling to room temperature, the S/CNT composite was obtained.
A 20 wt.% aqueous ethanol (EtOH, 99.7%, Shanghai Rongrun Chemical Reagent Co.) solution was prepared by mixing EtOH with deionized water.

S@C cathodes were fabricated as follows: The S/CNT active material, conductive additives (Super P (battery-grade, Termeco GMBH): CNT: graphene (battery-grade, Knano Graphene Technology Co.) at 6:2:2 mass ratio), and LA133 binder (battery-grade, Sichuan Indigo Technology Co.) were mixed in the EtOH solution at 8:1:1 mass ratio to form a slurry with 25 wt.% solids content.
The slurry was coated onto aluminum foil and dried at 80 °C for 6 h.
The sulfur content in the final electrode was 64%, with sulfur loadings of 1.1, 4.1, and 6.2 mgs cm−2 for electrochemical testing.
Materials Characterizations Solutions containing Li2S8, Li2S6, and Li2S4 were prepared by dissolving S/Li2S mixtures (molar ratios: 7:1, 5:1, and 3:1) in DOL/DME or CPME/DME solvents.
Phase separation behavior during aging was documented using a high-resolution digital camera.
To determine the composition of co-existing phases, saturated Li2S8 solutions were prepared in various solvents.
After sampling, volumetric dilution, and quantitative analysis, sulfur content was measured by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES, ICPOES7200, Thermo Scientific, USA).
Ionic conductivity of electrolytes was characterized using a conductivity meter (DDS-307A, INESA Scientific Instrument Co., China).
Dynamic viscosity of prepared electrolytes was evaluated at 25 °C with a digital rotational viscometer (NDJ-9S, Lichen Bangxi Instrument Technology Co., China).
All physicochemical properties in this work, including density, sulfur content, ionic conductivity, and viscosity, represent mean values derived from three independent measurements.

Ionic and molecular coordination information in different electrolytes was characterized by Raman spectroscopy using a 532 nm laser (Renishaw InVia reflex, Renishaw plc, UK) and Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy (VERTEX 80v, Bruker Corporation, UK).
To observe the morphology and composition of the SEI on lithium anodes, Li-S batteries were disassembled after 50 cycles.
Lithium anodes were rinsed three times with pure DME to remove residual electrolytes and thoroughly dried within the glovebox.
Prior to SEM, XPS, and TOF-SIMS testing, electrodes were preserved in custom-made argon-filled containers to prevent air exposure during transfer.
Morphological characterization was performed using scanning electron microscopy (Regulus 8100, Hitachi, Japan) at 15.0 kV accelerating voltage.
Chemical composition of the SEI was analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (PHI 5000 VersaProbe III, ULVAC-PHI, Japan) with Al Kα radiation.
TOF-SIMS depth profiling (PHI nanoTOF II, ULVAC-PHI, Japan) was conducted in negative ion mode, where secondary ions were generated using a 2 keV Cs+ ion beam for surface sputtering.
Compositional depth profiling employed a pulsed 30 keV Bi3+ primary ion beam in high-current mode, with sputtering and analysis areas of 400 × 400 μm2 and 100 × 100 μm2, respectively.
All 17O NMR spectra were acquired on a JNM-ECA600 spectrometer using deuterated chloroform (CDCl3) as solvent.
The resonance frequency for 17O was 81.34 MHz with 2000 scans and a relaxation time of 1 s. 7Li NMR measurements were performed at 233.18 MHz with 64 scans and a relaxation time of 5 s.
All experiments were conducted at ambient temperature.
Electrochemical measurements Li-S coin cells were assembled in a standard 2025 coin cell battery.

To evaluate cycling performance and shuttle current, the following configurations were tested under mild conditions: low-loading sulfur cathode (1.1 mgS cm−2, 12 mm diameter), thick Li foil anode (400 μm, 16 mm diameter), a high electrolyte/sulfur loading ratio (E/S = 60 μL mgS−1), and polypropylene (PP) separator (Celgard 2500, 19 mm diameter).

Charge/discharge tests were performed using a Neware battery test system (MIHW-200-160CH-B, Shenzhen, China) in constant current mode at 0.2C and 0.5C rates (1C = 1600 mA g−1) over a voltage range of 1.7–2.6 V.

Under practical conditions, the performance of the battery was tested at a current density of 0.1C and a constant temperature of 25 °C using a high-capacity sulfur cathode (4.1 mgS cm−2), a thin Li foil anode (50 μm) and a low electrolyte/sulfur loading ratio (E/S = 6 μL mgS−1).
In order to analyze the morphology and composition of the SEI on the surface of the Li anode, the battery was disassembled after 50 cycles.
Li||Cu cells were assembled in a standard 2032 coin cell battery and tested with a current density of 0.5 mA cm−2 and a surface capacity of 1.0 mA h cm−2.

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were conducted using an electrochemical workstation (Zennium XC, Zahner Elektrik, Germany) with a frequency range of 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz and a perturbation amplitude of 5 mV.

Cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves of pure solvents were measured using an electrochemical workstation (Zennium XC, Zahner Elektrik, Germany), with carbon-coated current collector as working electrode and lithium as counter electrode and reference electrode, at a scan rate of 0.2 mV s−1.
To measure shuttle currents, lithium-sulfur batteries were first charged to full capacity.

Using an electrochemical workstation (Zennium XC, Zahner Elektrik, Germany) in chronoamperometry (CA) mode, constant voltages were applied at 2.90, 2.60, 2.45, 2.43, 2.40, 2.39, 2.38, 2.37, 2.36, 2.35, 2.34, 2.25, and 2.20 V.
Due to polysulfide shuttle effects, the cell potential gradually decreases.
The steady-state current required to counteract this potential decay is defined as the shuttle current.
The in-situ Raman spectroscopy (LABRAM, HR) was tested with 785 nm laser excitation.
A three-dimensional current collector was employed for the cathode, and an additional carbon cloth was used as the electrolyte retention layer.
The Raman beams were focused on this electrolyte layer.
The Li-S visible cell was assembled in a H-type cell by using S/C (coated on the carbon cloth, area capacity 7 mA h cm-2) as cathode and Li metal (400 μm) as anode.
The current density of H-type cell is 0.7 mA cm-2, and the images were recorded based on the different points of the discharge curves.
Li-S pouch cells Li-S pouch cells were assembled in a dry room with a dew point below -40 °C.

The single-layer pouch cells were assembled using a high sulfur-loading cathode (4.3 mgs cm−2, size 6.5 × 4.5 cm2), a Li-plated Cu foil anode (50 μm Li, size 6.7 × 4.7 cm2), a PP separator (Celgard 2500), and a low electrolyte/sulfur loading ratio (E/S = 7.5 μL mgs−1).
The battery is tested at a constant current charge and discharge rate of 0.05C in the voltage range of 1.7–2.6 V.

Multi-layer pouch cells (1.8 Ah) were assembled using four-layer stacks of high-loading sulfur electrodes (the loading of each side is 6.2 mgs cm−2, size 6.5 × 4.5 cm2), five-layer stacks of thin Li foil anode (the loading of each side is 50 μm Li, size 6.7 × 4.7 cm2), PP separator (Celgard 2500), and low electrolyte/sulfur loading ratio (E/S = 3 μL mgs−1).
The battery is tested at a constant current charge and discharge rate of 0.05C in the voltage range of 1.7–2.6 V.
All pouch cell tests are performed in a 25 °C incubator.
Theoretical calculations Materials Studio software was used for theoretical simulation calculations in this work.

DMol3 module was used to perform DFT calculations to optimize the structure of ions and solvent molecules in different electrolytes, and calculate the electrostatic potentials and binding energy () of solvents and LiPSs.[1] The was calculated by the following formula: . , and were the total energy of the Li2S8-solvent, single Li2S8 and single solvent, respectively.[2] Geometry optimizations were performed using the generalized-gradient approximation (GGA)/Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional and a double numeric polarization (DNP) basis set.[3] The convergence criteria was set to be 1.0 × 10-5 Ha for energy, 2.0 × 10-3 Ha Å-1 for maximum force, and 5.0 × 10-3 Å for maximum displacement.

Classical MD simulations were carried out using the Forcite package in Materials Studio.[4] Two amorphous cells were constructed for the Li2S8/DOL/DME with molar ratio of 10:144:100 and the Li2S8/CPME/DME with molar ratio of 10:90:100.

The COMPASSIII force field was applied, with atom types and partial charges optimized based on previously validated studies.[5,6] The system was first equilibrated in the NPT ensemble for 50 ps (picoseconds) with a time step of 1.0 fs (femtoseconds) under controlled thermodynamic conditions.
A Nosé-Hoover thermostat and a Parrinello-Rahman barostat were ultilized[7,8], with the following setting: Cell time constant: 1.0 ps; Compressibility: 4.5 × 10−5 GPa−1; Coupling mode: Isotropic.
The simulations were conducted at 298.15 K and 1 bar.
Following equilibration, production runs were carried out in the NVT ensemble, maintaining the temperature at 298.15 K using the Nosé-Hoover thermostat.
A 1.0 fs time step and a total simulation duration of 2 ns were employed.
